As a brave Emberling, your mission is to rebuild your home in the heart of an ancient forest. To succeed, you'll explore the wilderness, gather resources, clear dangerous areas, and construct new homes for your kin. Along the way, you'll recruit heroes into your fellowship, each bringing unique skills that will help empower your team. Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 How to Play – Emberleaf 1.1 Core Actions 1.2 Actions in the Game 1.3 Scoring 1.4 Game End How to Play – Emberleaf Recruit the best fellowship of Emberlings as you rebuild the forest and win the hearts of your people. The Emberling with the most points at the end of the game wins. Core Actions On your turn, choose one: Play a hero card : Activate its on-play skills and add stats to your fellowship. Slide cards : Move every card on your fellowship board one space to the left, triggering slide skills. When a card slides off the board, it triggers drop-off skills and returns to your hand. Actions in the Game Walking: Move around the forest to position yourself for key actions. Moving from one clearing of the map to another requires 1 walk if the path is clear, and 1 extra walk if it's a dangerous path. Gathering: Collect wood, food, stone, and beehives to support your actions. You can hold up to 8 resources at a time (12 if the boat house next to your resource bank has been built). Attacking: Use attack skills to clear nearby dangerous areas, collect war banners, and advance the war banner track. The attack strength needed to clear a path is shown on the path token. Building: Spend resources to construct buildings in your current clearing, or upgrade your fellowship with special buildings. Building something will allow you to immediately home a villager. Homing: Place villagers in buildings to unlock bonuses, upgrade your fellowship, or activate scoring objectives. Each villager will give you a one-time bonus once it is homed. Favours: Collect up to 8 favour cards and complete their objectives. Favours are usually earned by visiting a clearing for the first time (but can be earned other ways). Scoring Earn points by: Connecting different types of buildings : When you home a villager, count how many unique building types containing one of your villagers are connected to each other. Score that many points. Clearing dangerous areas : When you clear a path, score points equal to the number of points given on that path. Collecting trophies : When you clear a path, the war banner advances to the next row on its track. The last row on this awards a trophy. Each of these trophies will score points, or give some other bonus action or resources (and in some cases, give other players a smaller reward). You can also earn a trophy when any clearing has all possible building sites built. Completing favours : All of your favours give conditional points at the end of the game. Game End The game ends after all six trophies have been awarded. [Rating: 3/10] Some neat ideas, and some terrible ones. It just takes twice as long as I would want it to.  While waiting for others to finish their neverending chain of actions, I kept forgetting what I wanted to do on my turn, and after a while I honestly stopped caring.

[Rating: 3/10] Not a fan of game design that force you to play a certain way.  Game is very cute and well produced but I Didn’t enjoy and game overstayed its welcome

[Rating: 3/10] Not bad, just forgettable with no urge to play agin, if someone else suggests it though we're good

[Rating: 3.5/10] Maybe worth a look for the “card dancing” system: cards are played to a grid where they usually have an placement action; alternatively, a player can take a slide action to move all cards left, potentially activating both on the slide and when falling off the left. Combo builders will enjoy making this sing.  This is married to an uninteresting, overlong and underbaked (if delightfully produced) game further ruined by the excessive impact of luck in the scoring and hero cards.

[Rating: 4/10] I really wanted to like this game, but unfortunately it just feels underdeveloped and poorly balanced.   The act of playing the game is pleasant enough, with the rules themselves being relatively easy to learn. There's a unique card-sliding mechanism that requires a bit of puzzling to truly capitalize on, and most of the gameplay comes down to choosing what order to play cards and slide them to be the most efficient. It's a great idea.  However, some very strong engine-building elements are tied to a limited resource (honey), which can easily be acquired at the start of the game by players ear
